opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest benefit is that physics trains a particular kind of taste: a sense for what the *right* simplification is. When you study physics, you're constantly confronted with systems that are hopelessly complicated if you try to describe every detail. The whole art is figuring out which few degrees of freedom actually matter, writing down the simplest model that captures them, and then being honest about where that model breaks. That habit of asking "what's the essential structure here?" turns out to be very transferable.

The second thing is comfort with first-principles reasoning. In physics you're encouraged not to just accept a result because someone important said it. You derive it, or at least you try to understand why it *has* to be true, often from symmetry or conservation arguments. That gives you a certain confidence, and sometimes a healthy stubbornness, when you move into a new field. You're not intimidated by the jargon, because you assume that underneath it there's a simple idea you could reconstruct yourself.

Third, physics teaches you to hold rigor and intuition at the same time. Mathematicians care deeply about rigor, while engineers care about what works. Physicists live in between. We'll do a calculation that's not fully justified, check it against limiting cases, estimate orders of magnitude, and decide whether it's believable. That back-and-forth between sloppy, fast intuition and careful verification is something I've found extremely useful later, including in AI research, where a lot of the work is empirical and you need good instincts about which experiments are worth running.

And finally, maybe more personally, physics gives you a sense of the beauty of understanding. When you see, for example, how a huge range of phenomena follows from a few principles, you get a kind of aesthetic standard. Later, when you work on something messier, you still carry that standard with you. You keep looking for the explanation that feels inevitable rather than just a collection of tricks. Even when you don't find it, I think searching for it makes you a better researcher.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest thing physics gave me wasn't any particular piece of knowledge. It was a way of thinking about problems that I still use every day, even though I left physics a long time ago.

The first part is what I'd call first-principles thinking. In physics you're trained to ask: what is actually going on here, underneath? What are the few fundamental things that everything else follows from? You don't accept a phenomenon as given, you try to derive it. And once you have that habit, it transfers to anything. When I started working on language models and agents, a lot of what was happening in the field looked like a pile of tricks and benchmarks. The physics instinct is to step back and ask, what is the real variable here? What is the mechanism? Is this a genuine effect or an artifact? That kind of question is uncomfortable to ask, but it's the only way to see past the noise.

The second part is comfort with abstraction and simplification. Physicists are famous for the spherical cow, right? You throw away almost everything about a system and keep only what matters, and you accept that the model is wrong in detail but right in essence. That sounds like a joke, but it's actually a very deep skill. Knowing what to ignore is harder than knowing what to include. A lot of good research, in AI too, is just choosing the right simplification, finding the toy problem that captures the real difficulty without the irrelevant complexity.

The third thing is a certain taste for elegance. In physics you develop a sense that if an explanation is ugly, it's probably not the final answer. Nature tends to be simpler than our first description of it. I think that taste matters a lot when you're choosing which problems to work on and which ideas to pursue. It's hard to articulate, but it's a kind of compass.

And honestly, there's a humility that comes with it too. Physics shows you very quickly how much smarter the universe is than you are. You build a beautiful theory, you run the experiment, and nature says no. You learn to let the world correct you rather than argue with it. In AI research that's enormously useful, because the field moves fast and your intuitions are constantly being falsified. People who come from physics tend to handle that pretty well, I think. They've already been humbled.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say physics teaches you how to think clearly about hard things, how to simplify without lying to yourself, and how to stay honest when reality disagrees with you. Those are useful far beyond physics. For me they turned out to be the most useful things I learned in college.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest benefit is learning how to turn a complicated phenomenon into a simple model. You have to ask: What are the important variables? What can I ignore? And under what conditions is that simplification valid? That’s a very useful way of thinking, even when you’re working on something far outside physics.

Another benefit is moving between intuition and mathematical reasoning. You might have an intuitive picture of how something works, but then you need to make it precise and see whether the consequences actually agree with observation. If they don’t, you have to change the picture. That back-and-forth teaches you both rigor and humility.

For me, that’s the lasting value of studying physics: developing the ability to build an explanation, understand its assumptions, and recognize where it stops working.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest benefit is learning to look for the essential structure of a problem. The world is very complicated, but in physics you ask: What are the important variables? What can I ignore? What is the simplest model that still explains what I’m seeing? That habit is useful far beyond physics.

You also learn to move between intuition and mathematics. You might have an intuitive picture, but you need to make it precise enough to derive consequences. Then you check whether those consequences make sense. If they don’t, you have to reconsider either the calculation or the original intuition.

And there’s a certain humility in that process. A beautiful explanation can still be wrong. Studying physics trains you to be comfortable with uncertainty while continuing to ask questions you can actually make progress on.
